content: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is a peptidyl dipeptidase that facilitates the conversion of angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor. Angiotensin II also stimulates the secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Inhibition of ACE leads to a reduction in plasma angiotensin II levels, which results in decreased vasopressor activity and reduced aldosterone secretion. This reduction in aldosterone may cause a slight increase in serum potassium levels, typically around 2 mEq/L. Additionally, the removal of angiotensin II's negative feedback on renin secretion leads to an increase in plasma renin activity. In animal studies, benazepril did not inhibit the vasopressor response to angiotensin II and did not interfere with the hemodynamic effects of autonomic neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine. ACE is biochemically identical to kininase, an enzyme responsible for degrading bradykinin. Bradykinin is a potent vasodepressor peptide, but its role in the therapeutic effects of Lotrel remains unclear. The primary mechanism by which benazepril lowers blood pressure is believed to be the suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. However, benazepril also demonstrates antihypertensive effects in patients with low-renin hypertension. Amlodipine, on the other hand, is a dihydropyridine calcium channel antagonist (or slow channel blocker) that inhibits the transmembrane influx of calcium ions into vascular smooth muscle and cardiac muscle. Experimental data suggest that amlodipine binds to both dihydropyridine and nondihydropyridine binding sites. The contractile processes of cardiac and vascular smooth muscle depend on the movement of extracellular calcium ions into these cells through specific ion channels. Amlodipine selectively inhibits calcium ion influx across cell membranes, with a greater effect on vascular smooth muscle cells than on cardiac muscle cells. While negative inotropic effects can be observed in vitro, these effects have not been noted in intact animals at therapeutic doses. Serum calcium concentrations remain unaffected by amlodipine. Its interaction with calcium channel receptors is characterized by a gradual rate of association and dissociation, resulting in a slow onset of effect. Amlodipine acts as a peripheral arterial vasodilator, directly targeting vascular smooth muscle to reduce peripheral vascular resistance and lower blood pressure. Lotrel is a combination of amlodipine besylate and benazepril hydrochloride. Benazepril hydrochloride is a white to off-white crystalline powder that is highly soluble in water, ethanol, and methanol. Benazeprilat, the active metabolite of benazepril, is a nonsulfhydryl ACE inhibitor formed through hepatic cleavage of the ester group in benazepril. Amlodipine besylate is a white to pale yellow crystalline powder that is slightly soluble in water and sparingly soluble in ethanol. It is the besylate salt of amlodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. The inactive ingredients in Lotrel capsules include calcium phosphate, cellulose compounds, colloidal silicon dioxide, crospovidone, gelatin, hydrogenated castor oil (not present in 5/40 mg or 10/40 mg strengths), iron oxides, lactose, magnesium stearate, polysorbate 80, silicon dioxide, sodium lauryl sulfate, sodium starch glycolate (potato), starch (corn), talc, and titanium dioxide. Single and multiple doses of 10 mg or more of benazepril inhibit plasma ACE activity by at least 80%-90% for at least 24 hours post-dosing. Within four hours of a 10-mg dose, pressor responses to exogenous angiotensin I are inhibited by 60%-90%. In patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension, benazepril reduces both supine and standing blood pressure to a similar extent without causing compensatory tachycardia. Symptomatic postural hypotension is rare but may occur in patients who are saltand/or volume-depleted. The antihypertensive effects of benazepril are not significantly different in patients on highor low-sodium diets. In normal human volunteers, single doses of benazepril increase renal blood flow without affecting the glomerular filtration rate. In hypertensive patients, therapeutic doses of amlodipine induce vasodilation, leading to reductions in both supine and standing blood pressures. These decreases are not accompanied by significant changes in heart rate or plasma catecholamine levels with chronic dosing. With once-daily administration, the antihypertensive effects of amlodipine are sustained for at least 24 hours. Plasma concentrations correlate with its effects in both young and elderly patients.
